==Problem==

Real numbers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are chosen independently and uniformly at random from the interval <math>[0,1]</math>. Which of the following numbers is closest to the probability that <math>x,y,</math> and <math>1</math> are the side lengths of an obtuse triangle?

<math>\textbf{(A)} \text{ 0.21} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \text{ 0.25} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \text{ 0.29} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \text{ 0.50} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \text{ 0.79}</math>

== Solution 1== 
The Pythagorean Inequality tells us that in an obtuse triangle, <math>a^{2} + b^{2} < c^{2}</math>. The triangle inequality tells us that <math>a + b > c</math>. So, we have two inequalities:
<cmath>x^2 + y^2 < 1</cmath>
<cmath>x + y > 1</cmath>
The first equation is <math>\frac14</math> of a circle with radius <math>1</math>, and the second equation is a line from <math>(0, 1)</math> to <math>(1, 0)</math>.
So, the area is <math>\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac12</math> which is approximately <math>\boxed{\textbf{(C)} ~0.29}</math>

==Solution 2 (Trig)==

Note that the obtuse angle in the triangle has to be opposite the side that is always length <imath>1</imath>. This is because the largest angle is always opposite the largest side, and if two sides of the triangle were <imath>1</imath>, the last side would have to be greater than <imath>1</imath> to make an obtuse triangle. Using this observation, we can set up a law of cosines where the angle is opposite <imath>1</imath>:

<cmath>1^2=x^2+y^2-2xy\cos(\theta)</cmath>

where <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> are the sides that go from <imath>[0,1]</imath> and <imath>\theta</imath> is the angle opposite the side of length <imath>1</imath>.

By isolating <imath>\cos(\theta)</imath>, we get:

<cmath>\frac{1-x^2-y^2}{-2xy} = \cos(\theta)</cmath>

For <imath>\theta</imath> to be obtuse, <imath>\cos(\theta)</imath> must be negative. Therefore, <imath>\frac{1-x^2-y^2}{-2xy}</imath> is negative. Since <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> must be positive, <imath>-2xy</imath> must be negative, so we must make <imath>1-x^2-y^2</imath> positive. From here, we can set up the inequality
<cmath>x^2+y^2<1</cmath>
Additionally, to satisfy the definition of a triangle, we need:
<cmath>x+y>1</cmath>
The solution should be the overlap between the two equations in the first quadrant.

By observing that <imath>x^2+y^2<1</imath> is the equation for a circle, the amount that is in the first quadrant is <imath>\frac{\pi}{4}</imath>. The line can also be seen as a chord that goes from <imath>(0, 1)</imath> to <imath>(1, 0)</imath>. By cutting off the triangle of area <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> that is not part of the overlap, we get <imath>\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2} \approx \boxed{\textbf{(C)} ~0.29}</imath>.
